content.title: Who will win (and who should win) at the 2026 Oscars
content.text: We did it, everyone. We made it to the end of Oscar season. I’m not saying this awards season was too long and grueling, but I’m just saying that I believe Stephen King used it as the inspiration for “The Long Walk” – complete with everyone kinda just wanting to be put out of their misery at some point. (I’m sure the BBC and BAFTAs in particular feel that way considering whatever the heck THAT whole situation was. It was more than a travesty. It was more than a debacle. It was a trabacle.)This sense of weary exhaustion at the finish line is a shame because, thanks to this needlessly long march, we’ve lost sight of how fun and good this year’s Academy Awards are. No one’s trying to ruin the show by eliminating categories, insulting nominees, and deleting hosts. There’s not really a true villain movie that people are dreading to see win – “Hamnet” is your closest culprit there, but even that’s viewed as more quaint than sinister – and there’s no nasty narratives infesting the show. Not even a single Karla Sofia Gascon tweet! (Wait, she posted something about the Timothee Chalamet “controversy”? Dammit, we were so close!) And best of all … basically all the movies are good! A year where the worst notable nominees are “F1: The Movie” and “Hamnet” is a year worth celebrating indeed. And when it comes to the main two front-runners, for cinephiles, studio heads, and average filmgoers alike, it’s the rare opposite of an “Alien vs. Predator” scenario: Whoever wins, we win.Indeed, just move the ceremony date up to not a quarter of the way into a whole new year, and the vibes would be terrific going into Oscar night. The box office is back! Hollywood made good movies! Everything’s fixed and nothing bad is on the horizon! Now, to take a quick sip of coffee and see what’s new with the iconic major studio behind the two Best Picture favorites … Well, let’s just politely ignore that existential nightmare that makes “Sirat” seem like a new Paddington movie and focus instead on the Oscar race – which, in a rarity, is actually still a race across most of the categories. Thanks to the rise in precursor attention these days, normally things are pretty locked into place, and it’s a march to the inevitable – but chaos reigns in 2026, and the Academy Awards are no different. So let’s make a misguided attempt to predict the chaos and make my annual guesses for who will be crowned come Sunday night.Will win: “Sinners”Should win: “Sinners”Let’s start with the nominees who can happily hit the open bar without fear of a public speaking part on Sunday night. As the obvious final nominee to crack the ten, the cliche but crowd-pleasing “F1: The Movie” is just happy to be there along with “The Secret Agent” and “Sentimental Value,” the two foreign language successes that never quite reached that top-tier level of buzz and acclaim to transcend voters’ language barriers and pull a “Parasite.” Their real Best Picture race will be in Best International Film. Even if “Bugonia” wasn’t too weird and divisive, the dark conspiracy drama feels like it came out too long ago – but then again, everything about this year’s Oscars feels like forever ago. “Marty Supreme” is too manic, while “Train Dreams” is too small and quiet – and the Netflix of it all makes it feel even smaller and quieter. And speaking of Netflix, “Frankenstein” … well, “Frankenstein” just isn’t good enough, especially when Guillermo del Toro already won Best Picture for a more universally lauded genre movie not all that long ago. Then there’s “Hamnet,” the closest thing this year has to a villain thanks to its old-school Oscar prestige energy and emotional insistence. Even though it’s the least of the nominees for me, it certainly has its fans – so much so there was a brief moment where I genuinely thought it might sneak through a split vote between the cool kid movies “Sinners” and “One Battle After Another” to claim a shocker victory. Much like “Frankenstein,” though, Chloe Zhao’s won recently for better – and more important, the precursor receipts just aren’t there. Other than the Golden Globes, voted on by non-Academy members, it just hasn’t won much anywhere else. I stuck to the old Academy rules last year and went with the safe respectable handsome drama for adults (“Conclave”) over the young, thorny, edgy choice (“Anora”), and I was made into a fool. A FOOL! AND I SHANT BE FOOLED AGAIN! A For Your Consideration campaign for the Ice Cube “War of the Worlds” would’ve been less embarrassing.That leaves “Sinners” and “One Battle After Another,” one of the most charming head-to-head races we’ve had in a long time. Normally, the top two competitors for Best Picture are diametric opposites of each other, narrative counterpoints: the traditional “Conclave” versus the new school “Anora,” the small gritty indie “The Hurt Locker” versus the ultimate shiny blockbuster “Avatar,” the musical Hollywood fantasy of “La La Land” versus the grounded human drama “Moonlight,” the heavy war film “Saving Private Ryan” versus the light costume dramedy “Shakespeare in Love.” These two, though, are shockingly the exact same: They’re two risky non-IP movies for grown-ups, blending clear political and social commentary with genre-mashing big-screen entertainment, miraculously shepherded through corporate Hollywood by two auteur writer-directors taking big risky creative swings for more money than studios would likely prefer. And they both paid off, with success at the box office (“Sinners” more so than “OBAA,” but a $200 million worldwide gross from the director of “Inherent Vice” is a victory in its own right), in critics reviews, in the cultural eye, and now with the little gold men. They’re both the kind of large-scale Hollywood success story – on both a creative and financial level – the Academy wants to celebrate. They even come from the same studio: Warner Bros., or at least the last gasp of it. They’re so similar, I can’t help but think Sunday night will result in a split ballot, with the Academy wanting to shine a spotlight on both and therefore giving one movie its director prize and Best Picture to the other. When it comes to the Best Picture half of this split, all the logic points to “One Battle After Another.” The revolutionary dramedy has won a vast majority of the precursor awards, from the critics prizes to most of the guild trophies and the BAFTA (British Oscars) Best Picture. It has all the narratives – a political statement, a Hollywood success story, a writer-director getting long-deserved shine – while not feeling to voters like the boring or obvious pick. Meanwhile, we don’t talk enough about how strange this “Sinners” run is. A bloody, sexy, unapologetic genre movie released closer to last year’s Oscars than this year’s ceremony? That’s a collection of all the things that traditionally DON’T win Academy Awards, much less get nominated – and I know we’re in a post-Best Picture nominee “The Substance”/hot dog hands in a Best Picture winner world, but the old Academy is still in there somewhere. But I’ll be damned just like the vampires: I can’t help going with “Sinners.”“One Battle After Another” may have won most of the precursors, but “Sinners” won the most recent notable one: Best Ensemble at the Actor Awards (formerly the SAG Awards, a rebranding that makes a lot of sense but also I hate it) which is also the largest branch of the Academy. And the enthusiasm in the room came through my streaming screen. Thanks to that victory, Ryan Coogler’s film has the energy going into this final stretch – but it also had momentum at the start. After all, “Sinners” didn’t just get nominations: It got the MOST nominations, ever, with 16. Highly nominated movies can certainly have lowly trophy counts come the end of Oscar night; it feels like Scorsese’s last decade of movies all had handfuls of nominations only to result in empty hands, for instance. But breaking an almost century-long record – especially for such an unconventional Academy favorite, a spring-released horror movie – isn’t something that happens on accident without passion behind it. And considering Best Picture is decided by a preferential ballot, meaning the most beloved movie will fare better than the most merely liked, that passion literally counts for something.“Sinners” has defied the odds at every phase of its existence thus far – why not one more time? Will win: Michael B. Jordan, “Sinners”Should win: Timothee Chalamet, “Marty Supreme”I’m still at the energized phase of overwriting these picks, so let’s break all the options down here! Ethan Hawke’s certainly due for a win one of these years – and this fantastically verbose, practically one-man-show Lorenz Hart portrait would be a worthy way to earn it – but “Blue Moon” is probably too small and too outside of the general conversation to pull off the surprise. Wagner Maura would be worthy too, but “The Secret Agent” began to fly under the radar since nomination morning, and foreign language acting winners are rare. In Best Actor, it’s happened only once with Roberto Benigni – and I think the Academy’s still recovering from that. Elsewhere, it was hard enough to get Leonardo DiCaprio his first Oscar – they’re not giving him a second one this soon, and certainly not for one closer to goofball mode. This Leo talks brings us to Leo Jr., aka Timmy Chalamet. He’s great in “Marty Supreme,” a true movie star performance that made a period piece ping-pong dramedy a Christmas smash and that would be wholly intolerable if it didn’t balance the character’s chaos and charisma just right. But the Academy sure loves to make actors – especially the young ones – wait for their wins. And wait. And wait. And wait some more before they win for “The Revenant” or “Crazy Heart” or “Scent of a Woman” or some other performance we tolerate more than totally love. That was probably already Timmy’s fate – but then he fully clinched it when he gave his SAG speech last year about how he wants the awards and wants to be recognized as one of the greats. And if there’s one thing Academy voters love more than making actors wait, it’s making actors who REALLY want an Oscar REALLY wait. (Just ask Glenn Close.) Cue Timmy getting passed over last year – even for the good version of the kind of Oscar bait biopic performance that usually wins the long-delayed trophy 20 years from now – and cue Timmy getting passed over by both the BAFTAs and Screen Actors Guild after a promising campaign start. And that was all before … and I can’t believe I have to bring this up … Timmy Hates Ballet and Opera-Gate. I’m shocked, just shocked, that the internet is debating a famous person's inarticulate-but-accurate thoughts based on a quote being willfully pulled out of context. Doesn’t seem like the internet at all. It’s one of our dumber controversies – but unfortunately for Timmy, this excuse to be resistant broke out JUUUUUUUST in time for the Oscar voting window. Best of all, if voters – for rational or irrational reasons – find voting for Timmy harder to swallow than the garlic in “Sinners,” they have another quality place to redirect their vote: Michael B. Jordan. It’s a similarly compelling movie star performance – times two – in a surprise smash riding on his leading man shoulders, combined with a similarly compelling “crowning the next generation” awards narrative. And while a Timmy win feels inevitable to some, a Michael B. Jordan win feels invigorating – at least that was certainly the vibe when he won at the Actor Awards, a real pop in the crowd coming through. The Academy is obviously not above voting on vibes. Chalamet could certainly still win – like most of these categories, it’s excitingly still a contest after all this time – but with that SAG triumph, Jordan has the positive energy going into Sunday night. Meanwhile the only positive developments surrounding Timmy right now are record highs in affection for the ballet and opera arts. Will win: Jessie Buckley, “Hamnet”Should win: Rose Byrne, “If I Had Legs, I’d Kick You”Listen, they can’t all be fun, exciting, and unpredictable. Jessie Buckley’s been the front-runner for Best Actress since the start of Oscar season, and despite the best efforts of “The Bride!”, that’s how things have stayed. Part of her steamroller status is a fairly uncompetitive group of fellow nominees. Byrne’s great – and overdue for the recognition – but A24 barely gave “If I Had Legs, I’d Kick You” a real theatrical release much less a real campaign push. Emma Stone’s already won twice – all within the past ten years – and I doubt the Academy will graduate her to Meryl status in barely a decade’s time. Renate Reinsve’s “Sentimental Value” performance is quietly emotional and nuanced, but voters don’t usually do quiet and nuanced for their performance winners. And even though saying this puts my Wisconsin citizenship at risk, Hudson’s not winning for “Song Sung Blue” either. Her comeback narrative is fun, and she genuinely pops in a way she hasn’t in years, but voters aren’t thinking of single-nominee “Song Sung Blue” this late in the game, nor do I think they have the stomach to give a midwestern Neil Diamond cover band biopic one of its top prizes. It all just gives me Best Actor the year of “The Revenant” vibes, where everyone knew Leo was finally winning so everyone else kinda didn’t waste their time. Or that weird year where everyone just decided Renee Zellweger was winning again for a Judy Garland biopic that no one really liked or bothered thinking about again.But also, Buckley’s a steamroller because it’s exactly the kind of performance and narrative that becomes an Oscar steamroller. It’s a loudly emotional performance – the kind that its detractors would say is Most Acting rather than Best Acting – filled with big showstopper Oscar clip moments from an actress who’s been putting in quality work for a while and just needed the right showcase to reach this point. And while much has changed with the Academy in recent years, they haven’t changed THAT much that a grandiose howling performance with big cry moments in a literary-minded prestige costume drama isn’t EXACTLY that kind of role. I mean, “Hamnet” still got eight nominations. It may feel like an also-ran at this point but voters clearly appreciated it – and this is their place to recognize it. So congrats to Buckley – and in a rare situation, she can actually choose whether she wants the trophy or if she wants every DCP print of “The Bride!” deleted and melted out of existence. Tough choice! Will win: Sean Penn, “One Battle After Another”Should win: Benicio Del Toro, “One Battle After Another”At the start of this Oscar season, approximately around the start of the War of 1812, I thought this category was a total toss-up. Penn and Del Toro were both early favorites, but two contenders from the same movie risk splitting the vote – plus they both already have Oscars. Even those lukewarm on “Frankenstein” love Elordi’s physical and sensitive take on the monster, but again, the Academy tends to take its time to reward hot young actors on the rise. Giving Stellan Skarsgard the prize would be a great opportunity to both celebrate a respected acting vet and to spread the love and give “Sentimental Value” a win somewhere – but the buzz since his Golden Globes success died down fast. And Delroy Lindo’s surprise nomination seemed like the win at first, but as “Sinners” has picked up steam, so has his overdue narrative – even though it’s a fairly minor part. So it’s anybody’s game!But then, as the season went along, I realized: Oh, no it’s not. Of course Sean Penn’s winning. Sean Penn was always winning. A big, showy, tic-happy (in a good way) villain performance in the Best Picture frontrunner? Yeah, that’s the winner – even with two other trophies already in Penn’s pocket and the threat of a split vote. I’d love it if his co-star won instead – Del Toro’s steady resistance leader brings so much magnetic presence and warm soul to “One Battle” – but a performance that mellow was always gonna be a long shot. Oh well, we’ll always have a few small beers. Will win: Teyana Taylor, “One Battle After Another”Should win: Inga Ibsdotter Lilleaas, “Sentimental Value”Everything I said about Best Supporting Actor? Predicting the Best Supporting Actress category has been the insane inverse. At the beginning, Teyana Taylor seemingly had this award in the bag – but then something strange happened. After claiming the Golden Globe, she just … stopped winning precursors. First Wunmi Mosaku won the BAFTA, building on the momentum of her somewhat surprising Actor and Oscar nominations. So she became the favorite … for about five minutes, before Amy Madigan swiped that momentum by winning SAG’s supporting actress honor and charmingly chatting about the trophy’s Ken-like crotch on stage. So who knows what’s happening next! Maybe the “Sentimental Value” ladies will tie for the win at the end. Maybe Glenn Close will run on stage and finally snag her Oscar by force! (But really: A proper studio would’ve gotten her at least a nomination for “Wake Up Dead Man.”)So let’s make a doomed guess anyway! Even if the Oscars did gravitate toward quiet, observant performances, Ibsdotter Lilleaas is stuck competing against her co-star and therefore likely to split at least enough votes to fall short. Mosaku is very good (see also: 2020’s “His House”) but for better or worse, “Sinners” plays more like an ensemble movie than one of standout performances. And I know the Academy’s changed, but Madigan coming out of almost nowhere – truly, who even knew she was in “Weapons” when it came out? – to win for playing a tonally kooky villain in a bloody populist horror flick with no other nominations would be a shockingly unusual Oscar win for the ages. We’re not that far away from “Us” and “Hereditary” getting wholly blanked for significantly bigger performances from significantly bigger names.In the end, maybe I’m just being stubborn, but I’m sticking with Teyana. She absolutely electrifies the first act of the Best Picture betting favorite, a captivating performance that adds so much more beyond the page and hangs with the characters as well as the audience long after she bails from the film. The performance is great in a movie that’s great, the campaigning has been great, and her past resume’s great. (See “A Thousand and One!”) She’s got everything this season save for the wins – and she’ll amend that Sunday. To absolute ruin a quote from her performance, this Academy’s popping for her. Will win: Paul Thomas Anderson, “One Battle After Another”Should win: Ryan Coogler, “Sinners”Considering how tight things are between “Sinners” and “One Battle After Another,” you would think Best Director would be one of the most competitive awards of the bunch. Here it is, the ultimate showdown: Ryan Coogler versus Paul Thomas Anderson, the two overdue beloved writer-directer auteurs who guided two original visions of thoughtful entertainment through today’s creatively cautious studio system unscathed to box office success, critical esteem, and front-runner status. How is one supposed to pick between the two?! Oh … easily apparently, because PTA has pretty much swept all of the precursors this season, winning the Directors Guild Award, the BAFTA, the Critics Choice, the Golden Globe, just about them all. (OK, not ALL of them – he did miss out on the AARP Movies for Grownups Award.) Precursors don’t mean everything – but in the case of the DGA, it’s only strayed from the Oscars’ pick four times since Y2K. Underestimating Coogler and “Sinners” has been a great way to look like an idiot this past year, but this will be the rare case where the odds are accurately not in their favor.Will win: “One Battle After Another”Should win: “One Battle After Another”No need to overthink this: “One Battle After Another” – a truly exciting adaptation, taking source material and shaping it into something different, personal, and of-the-moment in a way that feels original in its own right – is one of two movies in the fight for Best Picture, and the other one is in the next category. But if we do NEED to overthink this, screenplay tends to be where the Oscars like to reward auteurs too cool to win the bigger prizes – Peele, Tarantino, Jonze, Jenkins, Almodovar, Kaufman, even PTA’s been more welcomed in these categories (six total nominations) than in direction (four nods) – and the four other nominees here are more respected for their aesthetic virtues than their scripted ones. There, overthinking finished – now I SUPER think it’s going to be Paul Thomas Anderson.Will win: “Sinners”Should win: “It Was Just an Accident”Voters aren’t going to let Sunday night pass without Ryan Coogler taking the stage – and if Best Picture’s up in the air, and Best Director feels locked up for PTA, then here’s where they’ll make sure he gets his well-deserved bow. Considering how much “Sinners” has been received as a victory for originality, it only makes sense to give him the award with “original” right there in the name. Will win: “Kpop Demon Hunters”Should win: “Zootopia 2”Netflix’s fizzy pop star sensation has dominated the past year, becoming the Big Red Streaming Monolith’s biggest movie ever. That’s right – even bigger than “Tall Girl!” It got so big, Netflix decided they actually wanted to make money off it and put it in theaters! And you know how much they hate that! So yeah, no amount of potential Academy snobbery will stop its Saja Boys-esque world domination tour from continuing on to the Oscar stage. Sorry, distant second place finisher “Zootopia 2” – you’ll just have to tolerate merely being the highest grossing American movie of 2025. Will win: “Sentimental Value”Should win: “The Voice of Hind Rajab”And now the award for Best Neon Movie (and also “The Voice of Hind Rajab,” which is an absolutely heartbreaking, enraging, and powerful work … but stands no chance coming late in the season from a tiny distributor, making this the rare case where a movie involving Brad Pitt, Joaquin Phoenix, Alfonso Cuarón, and Spike Lee is considerably the underdog). So of the remaining four, which flavor of Neon will voters choose? In the past decade, the winner here has been a Best Picture nominee seven times – so that wipes out Jafar Panahi’s terrific “It Was Just an Accident” and the existential desert rave thriller “Sirat,” which was probably always too edgy to score the trophy. That leaves us “The Secret Agent” and “Sentimental Value.” You underestimate the Brazilian vote at your own risk – but despite some early passion, the atmospheric Wagner Maura political drama hasn’t caught on the way “I’m Still Here” did last year. Maybe the momentum slowed because it’s more of a vibes-y immersive hangout drama than the thriller it seemed at face value, but come around nomination time, it didn’t snag the directing or writing nods that would show greater enthusiasm – nods that “Sentimental Value” DID score amongst its nine in total, quietly tied for the third-most nominated movie of the year. They’ll want to reward it somewhere, and here is the most logical somewhere. Will win: “Sinners”Should win: “One Battle After Another”New category alert! NEW CATEGORY ALERT! I haven’t been able to hit that big red alarm button since 2001 when the Academy finally got around to making a Best Animated Film category. And once again, they’re catching up to popular demand and creating an award for best stunt wor … wait, what’s that? It’s for casting while the stunts Oscar isn’t happening until NEXT year? Seems actively rude to do that just in time for the “Mission Impossible” franchise to be put on ice … but sure, casting’s fine too.Weirdly enough, this year’s so chaotic that the brand new award with no prior history to guide one’s guessing ISN’T one of the more unpredictable categories. Considering most voters have no idea what they’re particularly voting for here, they’ll likely vote for the movie they like the most – and if I had to guess, that’d be the one they just gave the most nominations of any movie in Academy Awards history. Plus, while you don’t deserve an award for the idea of “what if Michael B. Jordan but twice,” “Sinners” certainly deserves the prize for discovering Miles Caton. “One Battle After Another,” though, certainly could win for that logic, too. Plus it didn’t just find a new star in Chase Infiniti; it found out the Bud Light “Dilly Dilly” King could perfectly play a cold-blooded assassin.Will win: “Sinners”Should win: “Sinners”Sometimes precursor awards are a critical part of the prediction process … and then sometimes you just throw up the double bird to the guild awards and go with your gut. This is the latter. “One Battle After Another” won the American Society of Cinematographers’ big award this season – but the ASC Award lines up with the Oscar only about half the time. When the Academy as a whole gets their say, they tend to go with more bluntly flashy cinematography (“The Brutalist” over “Maria” last year, “Roma” over “Cold War,” “La La Land” over “Lion” in 2016). And as much as “One Battle After Another” looks great and has that hypnotic final chase, “Sinners” is more visually sumptuous in an overt way – and that’s not even including The Scene, which is exactly the kind of moment that can impress the voters who don’t even know what the word “cinematography” means. As silly as this sounds, there’s also that promo video where Ryan Coogler talked about the various aspect ratios incorporated into “Sinners” – and as much as that’s wholly irrelevant, the clip does a really good job of not only passionately explaining complicated technical elements but making sure the visuals are a part of the conversation and thought process around the movie. Is it a major factor? Absolutely not. But in a toss-up like this, subplots like that – or like the fact that “Sinners” cinematographer Autumn Durald Arkapaw could become the first woman of color to win this award in Academy history – can swing a few more votes in a certain direction. I mean, if any group would understand the value of everything inside and outside of the frame, it’d be cinematography, right?Will win: “One Battle After Another”Should win: “One Battle After Another”If “F1: The Movie” is this year’s “Ford vs. Ferrari,” then it could follow in its tread tracks and win – or it could be “Marty Supreme” and its now signature Safdie panic attack approach. But because many voters don’t tend to know what they’re supposed to be looking for here, Best Editing often overlaps with Best Picture – at least that’s been the case three years running now. Using that logic, this should be another “Sinners” success, but not only is the movie’s showstopper scene famously devoid of edits, I just have a hard time giving an editing award to a movie that cut its ending – not a cliffhanger or cute button, but a whole extended scene delivering the emotional completion of the story – into the end credits. So I’ll give it to its rival for the night, “One Battle After Another,” which nimbly ambles from tone to tone, segment to segment, while never once dragging across its almost-three-hour running time. Will win: “Frankenstein”Should win: “Sinners”We now interrupt the “Sinners” and “One Battle After Another” love-a-thon for the “Frankenstein” portion of the evening! I love the lived-in sweaty Southern gothic world of “Sinners,” but Guillermo del Toro movies exist to win these kind of technical production craft awards with their elaborate fantastical sets and his gorgeously macabre vision. (It helps that del Toro is so good at passionately talking about and showcasing these elements during campaign season, too.) “Frankenstein” got nine nominations, all the way up to a Best Picture nod, for a reason – and it was for exactly this kind of stuff. I mean, it certainly wasn’t for the frame story.Will win: “Frankenstein”Should win: “Sinners”I could probably just nicely copy-and-past the above paragraph since it’s basically the same story: “Sinners” has a great Southern period horror look – including the costumes – but “Frankenstein” has it beat in the gorgeous gothic department. “Sinners” costume designer Ruth E. Carter is a historic Oscar favorite who could make even more history Sunday night (a win would make her the first three-time Black Oscar winner), but “Sinners” just doesn’t have the lavishly detailed showstopper outfits that got her “Black Panther” wins across the finish line. The same goes for “Hamnet” and “Marty Supreme” – both lived-in and immersive but lacking a signature look to stand out to voters, namely those less engaged in these technical categories. “Avatar: Fire and Ash” has great looks too, but for many voters, they’re still confused how it got a nomination for costumes that don’t exist. (Even though they do!) So yeah, “Frankenstein” wins. His fur coat DID look very cozy. Will win: “Frankenstein”Should win: “The Ugly Stepsister”As much as I would love for the tapeworm from “The Ugly Stepsister” to become an ACADEMY-AWARD WINNING TAPEWORM, yeah, it’s “Frankenstein” again. “Sinners” could sneak in for a win here – but that’s simultaneously too traditional, in that it’s a pretty genre-standard bunch of bloody bites and nasty faces, as well as too gnarly for the Academy. I know “The Substance” won last year, but that feels like a very special case. Most of the time, they’ll go for transformations over ripped-out tracheas. Will win: “Sinners”Should win: “One Battle After Another”Yeah, sure, “Bugonia,” “Frankenstein,” and “Hamnet” are technically nominated here – but none of them are coming to the ceremony on Sunday with speeches. “Bugonia” is too strange and too out of the picture to contend (a strange thing to say about a Best Picture nominee, but it was gripping to that spot by its alien fingernails). I couldn’t tell you what the “Frankenstein” score sounds like – probably fine, I guess. And Max Richter’s “Hamnet” nomination is mostly riding the coattails of “On the Nature of Daylight,” the emotional core of the film’s big finale that also CAME OUT MORE THAN TWO DECADES AGO! Best Original Score, my arse – and if we are giving out score nominations for stealing this song’s valor, where was the nod for “Arrival”!? So that means we’re returning to the “Sinners” and “One Battle After Another” show previously in progress – and between the two, the nod goes to “Sinners.” Jonny Greenwood’s chaotic score perfectly captures the unpredictable tone of PTA’s film and blends so many great themes into the story – plus he’s overdue for a win – but music is so integral to the “Sinners” experience that I can’t see voters ignoring the work here. Now, are they thinking more of the songs than the score itself? Possibly – but two-time winner Ludwig Goransson co-wrote many of those too so fair enough.Will win: “Golden” from “Kpop Demon Hunters”Should win: “I Lied to You” from “Sinners”The inescapable pop phenomenon “Golden” is an absolute lock here – maybe even the biggest lock of the night. And that’s even with Diane Warren lurking, trying to finally claim a victory after 17 NOMINATIONS with an original song she wrote for THE DOCUMENTARY ABOUT DIANE WARREN.Will win: “F1: The Movie”Should win: “Sinners”Man, I used to know my sound categories so well: Sound mixing leaned toward music-heavy winners, while sound editing often went the way of war and action movies. Look at me, so savvy, so insider-y. But then they went and just had to go smash the two sound categories into one starting with 2020’s crop, and now I know nothing. NOTHING! OK, maybe something: The mixers seem to have lost the merger, with music movies like “Wicked,” “Emilia Perez,” “A Complete Unknown,” “Maestro,” “Elvis,” “Soul, “Belfast,” and “West Side Story” all going flat since the unification. (“Sound of Metal” did win in 2020, but that was more about the immersion than the music.) That mutes any hopes for “Sinners” or “Sirat” – and of the remaining three, I’ll take “F1,” the movie whose cars went vroom vroom so well it got a Best Picture nod. Will win: “Avatar: Fire and Ash”Should win: “Avatar: Fire and Ash”There are some decent nominees here – “Jurassic World Rebirth” stinks but at least the dinosaurs look good, “The Lost Bus” takes on the CGI gauntlet of digital fire with immersive aplomb, the slick technical achievements of “F1” are basically the reason why it’s a Best Picture nominee, and “Sinners” is not only top of voters’ minds but also gave us the true gift of not one but two Michael B. Jordans. But it’s important to remember: Only one nominee here has Payakan. And while “Fire and Ash” was a mild disappointment with critics and at the box office (where it OOOONLY made $1.5 billion – embarrassing), it wholly delivered on Payakan the space whale photorealistically wrecking future colonists. Oh, I suppose there’s the rest of its breathtakingly immersive “Avatar” world too that’s still head and shoulders above the special effects of any other blockbuster out there. But mainly this is for Payakan.
